1:
Henry lays the disaster at the door of a girl's vain curiosity. Dinah was, so far as appears, Jacob's only daughter, and therefore the mother's fondling; those children seldom prove the best or the happiest that are most indulged. Being solitary at home with none of her own age and sex to converse with, she went out to see the daughters of the land, to see how they dressed and how they danced and what was fashionable among them — perhaps at a ball, and perhaps unknown to her father. She went to see, Henry adds, yet that was not all: she went to be seen too, and it may be with some thoughts of the sons of the land. Wesley repeats the sentence and sets her age at fifteen or sixteen. The beginning of sin, he adds, is as the letting forth of water.

Calvin presses the same charge harder and makes it exegesis. Moses in part casts the blame of the offence upon Dinah herself when he says she went out to see the daughters of the land, whereas she ought to have remained under her mother's eyes in the tent; the virtue the proverb assigns to women, that they be keepers of the house, suits girls also. From that he warns fathers of families to keep their daughters under strict discipline, since if a vain curiosity was so heavily punished in the daughter of holy Jacob, not less danger hangs over weak virgins today. Clarke will not have the blame divided at all. Rendering the phrase literally, that Shechem spoke to her heart, he takes it as evidence that there had been no consent on Dinah's part, the whole an act of violence, and that she was now detained by force in Shechem's house, where she was still found when Simeon and Levi sacked the city.

On Shechem himself the readings converge more than one expects. Calvin observes that he did not, having once abused her, treat her with contempt as men use harlots, but loved her as a wife and did not object even to circumcision to have her — though the fervour of lust had so prevailed that he first subjected her to disgrace, and in that want of self-government he grievously sinned. Henry marks the same by contrast with Amnon, who hated the woman he had wronged. Calvin further finds a laudable modesty in his leaving the match to his father's authority, and turns it into a weapon: since Shechem under the guidance of nature asked his father to procure his marriage, the right of parents over their children is inviolable, and this fornicator alone is judge enough to condemn the Pope for breaking that bond. Keil glosses the kind speech as an attempt to comfort her with the promise of a happy marriage. Clarke corrects a misreading the English invites: Hamor was the prince of the country, Shechem only the prince's son.

Jacob's silence is read four ways. Gill supposes the report reached him from one of the maids who attended her, since she can hardly have gone alone, and calls this his first affliction in his own family, though not his last. Ellicott explains the silence as caution: Jacob was no match for the Hivites, and Leah's sons had the right to uphold their sister's honour. Calvin denies that he was deferring vengeance; alone and devoid of counsel and consolation, he lay prostrate as one disheartened, or else was restrained by prudence from making his feelings public before he was prepared to meet the danger. Henry hears in it a man astonished who knows not what to say, and adds an uncomfortable possibility, that he had left the management of his affairs too much to sons who had lately grown bold and assuming — for things never go well when the authority of a parent runs low in a family.
6:
The phrase folly in Israel draws the grammarians together. Wesley and Henry both note that it speaks the language of after-times, Israel being not yet a people but a family only; Ellicott makes the same observation an argument, that using Israel for the household as distinguished from the man belongs to the age of Moses and shows his hand in the weaving of these records. Clarke prefers to keep it contemporary by translating the preposition otherwise: not in Israel but against Israel, so that the offence is aggravated by being done against the prince of God himself, both names standing in the sentence — Jacob, whose daughter was defiled, and Israel, against whom the wrong was committed. Calvin reports that reading and then presses the clause that follows, which is commonly given as meaning that such a thing ought not to be done; in his judgment it describes the brothers instead, who had determined with themselves that the injury was not to be borne. Henry finds the doctrine in the name: uncleanness is folly, sacrificing the favour of God and peace of conscience to a brutish lust.

Henry is uneasy about the anger even so. The sons were influenced perhaps rather by jealousy for the honour of their family than by any sense of virtue, and many are concerned at the shamefulness of sin who never lay to heart the sinfulness of it. Calvin says it more bluntly by way of Hamor. Their indignation ought to have been mitigated by the old man's courteousness, who was prince of the city while they were strangers, and who offered equitable conditions and pleaded for his son; that they remained implacable is a sign of most cruel pride, since they were not moved even by the prayers of one who had wronged them through blind love and without malicious intention. Ellicott sets out what was actually proposed, that Jacob's family abandon their nomad life and settle, trading and acquiring not movable goods only but immovable property, the two clans coalescing into one community. Henry adds the comment that shames the story: in this treaty the Canaanites were the more honest of the parties.

On the dowry the lexicographers explain a custom. Gill notes that in those times a man did not receive a portion with his wife but gave one, to her or to her parents for her. Ellicott separates the two words: the mohar is the price paid to the bride's kindred though it takes the form of a present, the matthan the gift made to the bride herself. Shechem offers both without limit.

The answer that met this offer is condemned by everyone. Gill observes that though Onkelos, Jonathan and Jarchi render the word as though the sons answered with wisdom, it is never used in a good sense, and if it was wisdom it was carnal wisdom, disapproved by plain-hearted Jacob. Clarke says nothing could excuse it, yet notes that the parenthesis pleads provocation: they spoke so because he had defiled their sister. Henry allows the pretence was specious and would have been commendable if sincere, professors not being meant to marry the profane; but the Shechemites were to be circumcised not to make them holy, which was never intended, but to make them sore and so an easier prey to the sword — and bloody designs have often been carried on most securely under a pretence of religion, dissembled piety being double iniquity. Calvin adds the sacramental charge: they sever the sign from the truth it represents, as if a man might pass into the Church of God merely by laying aside his uncircumcision. Keil observes that the terms seemed reasonable to the two suitors, and that the note of Shechem's prompt compliance stands in the narrative by anticipation, before he had in fact gone down with his father to the gate.
18:
Henry and Wesley account for the two suitors' compliance charitably. They were moved not only by the strong desire to bring the match about but by what they may have heard of the sacred and honourable intentions of this sign in the family of Abraham — many who know little of religion, Henry adds, yet know so much of it as makes them willing to join themselves with those who are religious. Ellicott infers the same from their readiness: circumcision must have been a rite not only well known but reckoned honourable, or they would not so easily have submitted to a thing so painful. Gill divides the motive, Hamor moved by love of his son and Shechem by love of Dinah. Calvin is less kind to the father. He ought at the outset to have corrected his son's fault severely; instead he covers it and yields to every wish, and that an old man should for his son's sake adopt a new religion and suffer a wound in his own flesh cannot be acquitted of folly.

At the gate Calvin watches the argument being chosen. It was no light thing to bring a whole people to so great a change, so Hamor and his son reason from utility, which is natural rhetoric, since honour makes the more plausible appearance but is for the most part cold in persuasion, while among the common sort utility carries almost every point. They praise Jacob's household for honesty and quiet habits, urge that the land is wide enough for both, and conceal the private and real cause of the request, so that all these pretexts were fallacious. Calvin turns it into a standing complaint: men of rank commonly make everything serve their own ends while feigning care for the common good, so that hypocrisy appears so deeply rooted that it is a wonder to find anyone quite free of it; and let the people govern themselves too, lest they be caught by a specious show of good, as fishes are by the hook. Gill notes that the gate was where courts were held and city business transacted.

The bait itself is examined by four. Wesley states the calculation plainly: Jacob's sons were thriving people, and an alliance promised to improve trade and bring money into the country. Ellicott finds real plausibility in it, since in so young a community a large accession of women was a valuable increase of strength, and guests rich in cattle would raise Shechem high among the petty states of Canaan. Clarke calls it a bait held out to the unsuspecting people by their prince and his son, who were themselves not much less deceived. Henry allows the reasoning its force and condemns the principle: it was bad enough to marry on such a footing, covetousness being the greatest matchmaker in the world, and worse to be circumcised on it, since there are many with whom gain is godliness.

Clarke explains the town's obedience from the manners of the East, where petty princes have always been absolute and their subjects prompt and blind: the old man of the mountain answered an ambassador who required homage by bidding one attendant stab himself and another leap from the tower, then remarking that seventy thousand were thus attentive to his commands. Calvin grants that the consent looks like modesty and humanity, but holds that to change religion so carelessly betrays a gross contempt of God, since men who seriously worship do not cast aside their superstitions until convinced by sound doctrine: search the isles, says the prophet, and see whether any nation has deserted its gods, which yet are no gods. Henry says the same more shortly, that they submitted to serve a turn, to please their prince and enrich themselves, and that as nothing secures us better than true religion, so nothing exposes us more than religion only pretended to.
25:
Why the third day was chosen is answered from medicine. Gill says the pain of circumcision was sharpest then, the part more inflamed and the man more feverish, as physicians observe of other wounds — Hippocrates advised not to meddle with a wound on the third or fourth day, lest it rankle and bring on fever. Clarke says the same: the inflammation at its height and the fever following left the sufferer helpless, so the brothers came on the city unsuspected and in no danger of resistance. Calvin will not build on it: the Hebrews think the pain was then most severe, but he judges the proof neither valid nor of much moment. On how many struck he is more definite: though Moses names two, they were leaders of a troop drawn from a large household, and the deed is ascribed to them as Carthage is said to have been destroyed by Scipio. Clarke supposes the servants who helped with the flock were among them.

Calvin and Ellicott both make Leah the reason the two acted. Being her brothers by both parents, Calvin says, they were impelled less by the reproach brought on the elect race, of which they had lately boasted, than by the infamy brought on themselves. Ellicott guesses Reuben and Judah were shut out of the plot, the one as feeble and opposed to bloodshed, the other as too honourable; and against Henry, who reckons the pair young men not much above twenty, he holds they must have been of ripe manhood before they could have had influence enough for so terrible an exploit.

Henry lays out the aggravations, and Wesley repeats them almost verbatim. It should have been considered how far Dinah was accessory: had Shechem abused her in her mother's tent it would have been another matter, but she went upon his ground and perhaps struck the spark that began the fire — when we are severe upon the sinner we ought to consider who was the tempter. Shechem had done ill, but was endeavouring to atone, and was as honourable after the deed as the case would admit; And what was his sin to all the Shechemites? Does one man offend, and must the innocent fall with the guilty? Worst of all was the treachery, since they acted as sworn enemies towards men who had just become sworn friends, making as light of their covenant as of the laws of humanity: are these the sons of Israel? Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce. Henry adds a fifth charge Wesley drops, that they made a holy ordinance serve a wicked design and so brought reproach on the badge of their religion.

The plunder is treated as a second crime. Calvin reads the phrase about coming upon the slain either of making a way over the bodies or of adding spoil to slaughter, and says that from murderers they became robbers, since he who gives himself the rein in one wickedness soon breaks out into another. Wesley notes that the rest, by coming on the slain, made themselves accessory, and Clarke that two men could never have carried off the women, children and cattle unaided. Henry finds God's righteousness in the outcome, since the men who had asked shall not their cattle be ours lost their own instead: those who unjustly grasp at what is another's justly lose what is their own. Gill marks the retaliation too, and pities Shechem, who deserved better than the sword, while Hamor perhaps died for conniving at his son's sin. Ellicott corrects the rendering of the last item of spoil: the word is not little ones but the household persons, the men-servants and maid-servants, who would be the most valuable part of it. Keil notes what followed at once, that Jacob reproved the originators most severely for having made him an abomination among the inhabitants of the land.
30:
Jacob's complaint is heard first as a calculation of odds. Clarke paraphrases it as distress of mind and danger to his person: the deed has made him odious to the surrounding tribes, and when it gets abroad they will confederate against him and extirpate his family. Wesley presses the same arithmetic: though Jacob knew God had promised to preserve his house, he might justly fear that these vile practices would amount to a forfeiture and cut off the entail, for when sin is in the house there is reason to fear ruin at the door. Calvin observes that Moses records the rebuke lest anyone suppose the holy man had shared in the counsel, and that the Canaanites and Perizzites are named because, though they had suffered no wrong, they were by nature prone to inflict injury.

Whether so worldly a reproof was adequate divides the readers. Ellicott says plainly that it was not: Jacob's timidity led him to think first of the danger and only afterwards of the cruelty and treachery, so that his reproof is singularly weak and the retort of his sons just — though in avenging that wrong they had committed a crime of a deeper dye. Calvin raises the objection himself, asking why Jacob is not rather angry at their cruelty, offended at their perfidy, sharp against their rapaciousness, and answers it. Seeing them already terror-stricken, he probably suited his words to their state of mind, complaining as though it were he and not the Shechemites who had been killed; for men are seldom drawn to repentance except by fear of punishment, especially when they have a specious pretext to cover the fault. Clarke settles the question from elsewhere: the resentment was certainly not dissembled, since Jacob afterwards deprived these two sons of the birthright they would otherwise have enjoyed.

The sons' answer is judged by all of them and defended by none. Gill notes the pert and unseemly manner of it, and reports the Targums expanding the sense — that Shechem should not be left to boast of Dinah as of a harlot whom no man seeks to avenge — with the tacit insinuation that Jacob had not resented the wrong to his daughter as he ought. Wesley concedes the premise and denies the inference: no, he should not have dealt so with her; but must they be their own avengers, and could nothing less than a whole city atone for the abuse? Calvin finds in the two words both ferocity and stupidity: barbarous, that they excuse the destruction of a whole people by the injury of one man, answer their father so contumaciously, and obstinately defend a revenge rashly taken; and senseless, that they were untouched by the prospect of their own death and their families', which seemed at hand. Intemperate anger, he concludes, deprives men of their senses, and it is not enough to lay blame on our opponents unless we also see how far it is lawful for us to go.

Clarke ends with a lexicon and a reckoning. The word for harlot occurs here first, and is not the term rendered concubine but one meaning a woman who prostitutes herself for hire. Blame, he says, attaches to all parties: to Jacob, for suffering his daughter to go out alone; to Shechem most of all, though it would be unjust not to add that he wished to make every reparation in his power, and in that is a saint beside profligates who make none and glory in their shame; and to the brothers, whose act was diabolical. Of the religious cloak thrown over it he asks the obvious question and answers it: how often has the religion of God been made a covert for the worst of crimes — yet were it not so good as it is, it could not be so abused.
